title: Loved in God (4.12)
hookLine: if souls please thee, love them in God
tomorrow: what if the teacher you waited years for can't answer?

cards: After a breakup or a funeral, some people make a quiet rule: never get that close again. Is it safe to love after a grave like that? Augustine asks it outright.
He leaves his hometown, because every place there speaks of his friend, and goes to Carthage. Time does its slow work; new friends, talk, books read together.
Then he gives his answer, and on first hearing it sounds strange. If souls please you, he writes, love them in God. Is that a way of loving people less?

teach.b: The puzzle solves itself once you see what he blames. Not love. He'd poured out his soul on the sand, he says, loving someone who would die as if he never would.
The love wasn't too big. It had no ground under it.
So book four gives the fuller line: if bodies please you, praise God for them; if souls please you, love them in God. And here's his reason. People change, and on their own they pass away.
In God, he says, they stand firm. That's the key to the puzzle.

teach.h: NOT LESS LOVE: GROUND UNDER IT.
teach.b: Augustine isn't asking anyone to love their friends less, or to love God instead of them. He's saying where to set the love, so it has ground under it when people change or go.
He adds something that sounds like a friend's advice: God didn't make things and then walk away. They come from him and remain in him.
So loving a friend in God means seeing two things at once: this person, and the one who gave them. And the love doesn't stay private.
Augustine says to carry as many souls as you can along with you, and say to them, let us love him. Even the grief from yesterday turns out to be love looking for a place to stand.

how: Some Catholics read the Confessions slowly as spiritual reading, a few pages at a time. Augustine's idea of loving others in God is part of how the Church speaks about charity: love of neighbor held within love of God.

o: loving God so much that people come second
loving only the people who share your faith
loving people as gifts held in the one who made them

games.q: love with ground under it — tap the pairs.
p: where he'd poured out his soul
what he says to carry others along

s: loving people in God means loving them less
not less love: love set on ground that holds when people change or go.
Augustine blames his grief on loving too much
he blames loving a mortal as if he'd never die: love with no ground under it.
Augustine says God made things and remains with them
he didn't make them and walk away; they come from him and remain in him.

games.q: your friend's parents divorced, and she's decided never to depend on anyone again. what does Augustine's answer offer her?
o: love still, but set it on ground that doesn't move.
she's right: the safest heart is the one that never attaches.
love God instead, and let people go.
games.why: after his grief, Augustine doesn't stop loving people. he loves them in God, where, he says, they stand firm.

practice: Bring to mind one person you love, someone whose voice you'd know in a crowded room. Count three things about them you never earned: a laugh, a habit, a kindness.
For each one, let a small thanks rise, to God if you pray, or simply into the quiet.

wordCard.voice: Loved in God. Augustine's answer after grief: love people as they are, changeable, and love them in the one who made them and holds them.

orig.s: si placent animae, in Deo amentur
orig.say: see PLAH-chent AH-nee-meh, in DAY-oh ah-MEN-toor
orig.note: Latin, Confessions 4.12: if souls please you, let them be loved in God.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: love them in God, not less love but love with ground beneath it. Until tomorrow.
